title: Sentence Screen Fitting
statement:
A screen has `rows` lines, each exactly `cols` characters wide. Starting at the top-left, you write the words of `sentence` onto it in order, and after the last word you begin again with the first word, for as long as words still fit. Return how many complete copies of the sentence end up on the screen.

- Words keep their order and are never broken across two lines: when the next word does not fit in the rest of the current line, it starts the next line instead.
- Two words on the same line are separated by exactly one space; a line never needs a space at its start or end.
- A word longer than `cols` can never be placed, so writing stops there.
constraints: sentence[i] contains only lowercase English letters
signature: int wordsTyping(String[] sentence, int rows, int cols)
notes:
## Intuition

Writing word by word works but can take `rows · cols` steps. Instead, picture the sentence joined with single spaces and a trailing space, `"a bcd e "`, repeated forever. The screen shows a prefix of that endless string, row by row. Keep one counter `typed`: how many characters of the endless string are used so far. Each row first takes `cols` more characters, and then only the row's edge needs fixing, which costs at most one word's length.

## Approach

1. Build `text` = the words joined by spaces plus one trailing space, of length `length`.
2. For each row, add `cols` to `typed`.
3. If the next character, `text[typed % length]`, is a space, the row ended exactly at a word's end; skip that space (it is not needed at a line's end).
4. Otherwise the row cut through a word: move `typed` back until the character before it is a space, so the cut word starts the next row.
5. Each full copy of the sentence uses exactly `length` characters, so the answer is `floor(typed / length)`.

## Example 1, step by step

`text = "hello world "`, `length = 12`. Row 0: `typed = 8`; `text[8] = 'r'` is not a space, so back up past `'o'` and `'w'` to `typed = 6` ("world" moves down). Row 1: `typed = 14`; `text[2] = 'l'` is not a space, so back up past `'e'` and `'h'` to `typed = 12`. The answer is `floor(12 / 12) = 1`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(rows · w + total length), where w ≤ 10 is the longest word: each row backs up at most one word.
- Space: O(total length) for `text`.

## Pitfalls

- Use `%` on every index: `typed` runs far past `length`.
- Guard the back-up loop with `typed > 0`; when a word is longer than `cols`, `typed` falls back to where the row began and never moves on, giving 0.
- Skipping the space only when it falls right after the row is what allows a word to end exactly at the last column.
- Simulating word by word for each row is too slow when `cols` is large and the words are short.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `text` | the sentence joined by spaces, with a trailing space |
| `length` | the length of `text`: characters used by one full copy |
| `typed` | characters of the endless repeated `text` placed so far |
| `row` | the current screen row |

narration.2: Join the words with single spaces and add one at the end, so repeating this string models the endless text.
narration.3: Each full copy of the sentence uses exactly this many characters.
narration.4: Count how many characters of the endless text are placed so far.
narration.6: Fill the screen one row at a time.
narration.7: Optimistically take a full row of cols characters.
narration.8: Is the character just after the row a space? Then the row ended exactly at a word's end.
narration.9: Skip that space: it is not needed at the end of a line.
narration.11: Otherwise the row cut a word, so back up to the start of that word...
narration.12: ...one character at a time, so the word moves to the next row.
narration.16: Every length characters is one complete copy of the sentence.
